catalog_quote: Mij komt het voor dat men voor de vulgarisatie het belang van de tonen als volgt zou kunnen voorstellen : de hoge toon heeft in het Kesâkâtâ ongeveer hetzelfde belang als het krachtaccent in onze Europese talen. Vergelijkingen zijn nooit adequaat; zij helpen een gedeeltelijk en gebrekkig begrip te vormen van een totaal nieuw iets. ... Het krachtaccent integendeel lijkt mij in het Kesâkâtâ van zeer klein belang; alleen een rythmisch belang. Het is weinig merkbaar, niet sterk. Ongeveer gelijk aan de intonatie in een Europese taal. [Résumé, pp. 141-142:] Les racines des mots, après soustraction des éléments morphologiques variables, ont des tons invariables mais imprévisibles. ... On peut, toute proportion gardée, comparer le rôle des tons musicaux, à celui de l'accent tonique dans nos langues. ... L'accent tonique en Kesâkâtâ semble n'avoir qu'une importance purement rythmique.

new_statements.translation: It seems to me that, for popularization, the importance of the tones could be put as follows: in Kesakata the high tone has roughly the same importance as the stress accent in our European languages. [...] The stress accent, by contrast, seems to me of very little importance in Kesakata; only a rhythmic importance. It is barely noticeable, not strong. Roughly comparable to intonation in a European language. [Resume:] The stress accent in Kesakata seems to have only a purely rhythmic importance.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sakata is a two-level tone language with lexically unpredictable root tones; dynamic (intensity) stress is weak, non-distinctive and merely rhythmic. The source does not say on which syllable any such rhythmic prominence falls. (The only positional claim found is Guthrie 1948's zone-level 'stress on the radical syllable' for Zone B, which then included Sakata as B.44 -- second-hand/generic, reproduced in Tylleskar 1987 annex.)
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: high tones immediately before a pause are realized slightly lower ('pauzale toon'), treated as intonation, not a third toneme (pp. 140-142).
new_statements.domain_note: General characterization of the language (word-level tone vs. weak rhythmic stress); no citation-form vs. phrase distinction is drawn for stress. Tylleskar 1987 (Lemvien-Nord variety) independently confirms the tonal analysis (4 tonemes on CV radicals, H/L elsewhere) and is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: de Witte 1950 speaks of 'Kesakata' (the language of the Basakata) in general, from C.I.C.M. mission work in the Kutu territory; Tylleskar 1987 describes the Lemvien-Nord variety (Nioki area, central Sakata, close to Kingingia/Kimbantin). Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect glottocodes under saka1287; Maho/Guthrie subdivide C34A Sakata proper, C34B Dia (Kinzinzale/Wadia), C34C Bai, C34D Tuku/Tow. All statements here concern Sakata proper (saka1287).

sources.locator: p. 140 (section '2) Hoe de rol van de tonen moet opgevat worden'), with French resume p. 142; PDF text lines ~6231-6249 and ~6318
sources.note: Section 2 on the role of tones: root tones are lexical and unpredictable (two-level tone system); p.140: the high tone has in Kesakata roughly the importance that the stress accent has in European languages, whereas the stress accent ('krachtaccent') itself is 'van zeer klein belang; alleen een rythmisch belang. Het is weinig merkbaar, niet sterk'; French resume p.142: 'L'accent tonique en Kesakata semble n'avoir qu'une importance purement rythmique.' No statement of where stress falls. Also notes a slightly lower high tone before pause (intonation).

sources.citation: Tylleskar, Thorkild. 1987. Phonologie de la langue sakata (BC 34), langue bantoue du Zaire, parler de Lemvien Nord. Memoire de maitrise, Universite de la Sorbonne Nouvelle (Paris 3). 205 pp. (open PDF via NVA/Brage, Univ. Bergen).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Sec. 2.4 'Les tonemes' (printed pp. 104-108): 'La langue kisakata est une langue tonale', four tonemes (H, L, rising, falling) on CV radicals, only H/L on prefixes and CVCV/CVV radicals; pitch declines through the phrase. No accent/stress section; the word 'accent' does not occur in the description proper. Annex 3.3 reproduces Guthrie 1948 and 1953 (see separate entries).

sources.citation: Guthrie, Malcolm. 1948. The Classification of the Bantu Languages. London: OUP for IAI. Zone B chapter (Sakata = B.44), as reproduced in Tylleskar 1987 annex, pdf pp. 169-170.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Zone B 'Common Features' no. 13: 'Stress on the radical syllable. (Also in Zones C and H.)' -- a zone-level generalization, not a Sakata-specific observation (Sakata is cited by name only for other features: passives, vowel quantity ozo/ozo:, fused extensions, z/3/j alternance).
